about: Energieversorgung (370.002) and Maschinen und Antriebe (370.015) at TU Wien. Equations and worked examples of Energieversorgung after the lecture notes of Gawlik (2015), Skriptum version of 4 Oct 2015, cited by equation number and printed page, read in the notes' text layer on 1 Nov 2026; the slide sets V01–V22 of the same course (2015/16) are named for each part. Machines after Schrödl (2012), a scan: its equations were read from the page images on 1 Nov 2026 and are cited by equation number and printed page. Practice questions are the notes' worked examples or the worked solutions of the machines exams of 24 June 2013 and 24 July 2013 (in the students' collection 'VO-370.015 Prüfungen, Beispiele, Hybrid', 1 April 2017), each named; the rest were worked by hand from the equations and say so. tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes every answer with the core. Phasor arithmetic, Bode plots and control loops are the Automation lab's; harmonics and distortion power the Signals and systems lab's; waves on lines the Electrodynamics lab's.

labs.title: Star and delta
labs.idea: Three voltages of equal size, 120° apart. Between two lines lies their difference, √3 times longer. A load in star sees the smaller voltage and carries the line current; in delta it sees the line voltage, and each line carries the difference of two branch currents.

equations.eq: u_aN = Û cos(ωt + φ_u), u_bN = Û cos(ωt + φ_u − 2π/3), u_cN = Û cos(ωt + φ_u − 4π/3)
equations.note: a symmetric three-phase system
the rotation operator

equations.eq: U_bN = a² U_aN, U_cN = a U_aN
equations.note: each phasor the one before turned by 120°

equations.eq: 1 + a + a² = 0, a − a² = j√3
equations.note: so the three voltages sum to zero; a line voltage is √3 a phase voltage

equations.eq: 230 V line to neutral, 400 V line to line
equations.note: the Austrian low-voltage network, ±10 %

equations.eq: I_a = I_ab − I_ca
equations.note: a line current at a delta node, by Kirchhoff's current law

practice.question: Three branches of |Z| = 20 Ω are connected in delta to the 400 V network. What is the line current?
practice.solution: Each branch sees 400 V and carries 400/20 = 20 A. The line current is the difference of two branch currents 120° apart: √3 · 20 = 34.6 A. In star the same branches would carry 230/20 = 11.5 A, a third.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Gawlik (2015), (3-30) and (3-35)

practice.question: A star-connected network has 230 V from line to neutral. What is the voltage between two lines?
practice.solution: √3 · 230 V = 398.4 V, which the network names 400 V (table 3-2): the nominal values are rounded.

labs.title: Power in three phases
labs.idea: In one phase the power pulses at twice the frequency; its mean is the active power, its swing carries the reactive power back and forth. Three balanced phases add up to a constant: a three-phase machine sees no pulsating torque.
labs.law: S = 3 U I* = √3 U_n I_n (cos φ + j sin φ)
labs.lecture: Gawlik (2015), sections 3.1.3 and 3.2.3, pp. 36–43; slides V05+06

equations.eq: p(t) = U I [cos(φ_u − φ_i) + cos(2ωt + φ_u + φ_i)]
equations.note: one phase: a mean plus a pulse at twice the frequency

equations.eq: P = U I cos(φ_u − φ_i), Q = U I sin(φ_u − φ_i), S = U I*
equations.note: active, reactive and complex apparent power

equations.eq: S² = P² + Q²
p(t) = Σ u_k(t) i_k(t)
equations.note: three phases

equations.eq: P = 3 U I cos φ, Q = 3 U I sin φ, S = 3 U I
equations.note: symmetric system, line-to-neutral U

equations.eq: p̃(t) = Re{U_aN I_a (1 + a² + a) e^(j2ωt)} = 0
equations.note: the pulsating part vanishes in a symmetric system

equations.eq: S = √3 U_n I_n, P = √3 U_n I_n cos φ, Q = √3 U_n I_n sin φ
equations.note: with the line voltage U_n; φ is still between current and line-to-neutral voltage

practice.question: A symmetric load takes 50 A from the 400 V network at φ = 30°. What active power does it take?
And its reactive power?

labs.title: The transformer under load
labs.idea: Two tests describe a transformer: shorted, the voltage that drives rated current is its series impedance; open, the current is what magnetises its core. Under load the series impedance makes the secondary voltage sag, more with an inductive load, less or even upwards with a capacitive one.
labs.law: u_k = Z_k/Z_rT, u_r = P_k/S_rT, u_σ = √(u_k² − u_r²)

equations.eq: ü = U_rTOS/U_rTUS
equations.note: the ideal transformer's ratio

equations.eq: R_v = U_rTOS²/P_v, R_v ∥ ωL_h = U_rTOS/(√3 I_0)
equations.note: open-circuit test: iron losses and magnetising current

equations.eq: Z_k = U_kOS/(√3 I_rTOS), R = P_k/(3 I_rT²)
equations.note: short-circuit test, line voltages. The notes print (4-77) as R = U_kOS²/P_k, which (4-80) does not bear out; R here follows (4-80)

equations.eq: u_r = P_k/S_rT = R/Z_rT, u_k = U_k/U_rT = Z_k/Z_rT
equations.note: per-unit winding losses and short-circuit voltage

equations.eq: u_σ = √(u_k² − u_r²) ≈ u_k
equations.note: the inductive part; large transformers are nearly pure reactance
typical values

equations.eq: U₁² = |U₂ + (u_r + j u_σ)(P − jQ)/U₂|²
equations.note: the secondary voltage for a load P + jQ, a quadratic in U₂²; shunt branch neglected
circulating current of two paralleled transformers whose vector-group numbers differ by Δk

practice.question: A 110/30 kV transformer has S_rT = 31 MVA and u_k = 12 %. What is its short-circuit impedance on the 30 kV side?
Its short-circuit losses are 0.14 MW. What is its winding resistance on the 30 kV side?
A Yy0 and a Yd5 transformer of equal ratio and equal u_k are paralleled. How large is the circulating current, as a share of one transformer's short-circuit current?
practice.solution: ΔI/I″k = (1 − e^(−j5·30°))/2 = (1.866 + j0.5)/2, of size 0.966: about the short-circuit current, not allowed for long.

practice.question: A 1 MVA transformer (u_k = 6 %, u_r = 0.7 %, table 4-9) carries its rated power at cos φ = 0.8 inductive. By how many per cent does its secondary voltage fall?
practice.solution: u_σ = √(6² − 0.7²) % = 5.96 %. The first-order estimate u_r cos φ + u_σ sin φ = 0.56 + 3.58 = 4.14 %; solving U₁² = |U₂ + z I|² exactly gives U₂ = 0.9557, a fall of 4.43 %.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Gawlik (2015), (4-82) and table 4-9

labs.title: The long line and the Ferranti effect
labs.idea: A line is inductance in series and capacitance across. Open at its end, its charging current flows through its inductance and the voltage rises along it: at 800 km by half. Loaded, the voltage sags. At its natural load the two balance.
labs.law: U₂ = U₁ / (cosh γl + Z_w/Z₂ sinh γl)

equations.eq: γ = α + jβ = √((R' + jωL')(G' + jωC'))
equations.note: propagation constant
characteristic impedance, real for a lossless line

equations.eq: U₁ = U₂ cosh γl + Z_w I₂ sinh γl, I₁ = (U₂/Z_w) sinh γl + I₂ cosh γl
equations.note: the line equations

equations.eq: U₂ = U₁ / cosh γl
equations.note: an open line (I₂ = 0): the Ferranti effect

equations.eq: P_nat = U_n²/Z_w
equations.note: natural load

equations.eq: R' = 0.03 Ω/km, L' = 0.8 mH/km, G' = 0.02 µS/km, C' = 14 nF/km
equations.note: the notes' 380 kV line

practice.question: What is the natural load of the notes' 380 kV line (Z_w = 239.5 − j13.7 Ω)?
The line is 800 km long and open at its end; 380 kV are applied at its start. What voltage is at its end?
practice.solution: γl = (0.065 + j1.05)·10⁻³ · 800 = 0.052 + j0.84; U₂ = 380 kV / cosh γl = 567 kV, half again the start's voltage. (The notes print 152 %; 567/380 is 149 %.)

practice.question: The same 800 km line now feeds a resistance that takes 700 MW at 380 kV. What voltage is at its end?
practice.solution: Z₂ = (380 kV)²/700 MW = 206.3 Ω; U₂ = U₁/(cosh γl + Z_w/Z₂ sinh γl) = 322.5 kV at −50°, 85 % of nominal: too low.

practice.question: By how many per cent does the voltage rise at the end of 200 km of this line, open?
practice.solution: 1/|cosh γl| with γl = 0.013 + j0.21: 1.023, a rise of 2.3 %; at 500 km 16 %.

labs.title: Power over a line and voltage collapse
labs.idea: Active power crosses a reactance with the angle between its ends; reactive power with the difference of their voltages. Load the far end harder and its voltage sags until, at the nose of the curve, no more power can pass and the voltage collapses.
labs.law: P = U₁ U₂ sin δ / X

equations.eq: U₂ = U₁ − jX I₂, S₂ = 3 U₂ I₂*
equations.note: two networks joined by a reactance

equations.eq: P = 3 U₁ U₂ sin δ / X; maximum 3 U₁ U₂/X at δ = 90°
equations.note: active power and the pull-out power

equations.eq: Q = 3 (U₁ U₂ cos δ − U₂²)/X
equations.note: reactive power at the receiving end

equations.eq: U₂⁴ + (2QX − U₁²) U₂² + X²(P² + Q²) = 0
equations.note: per unit, δ eliminated: the PV curve

equations.eq: P_max = 3 U₁²/(2X) at δ = 45°, U₂ = U₁/√2
equations.note: a purely resistive load

practice.question: A resistive load is fed over a reactance of 0.5 p.u. from a busbar held at 1 p.u. What is the most power it can draw?
practice.solution: P_max = U₁²/(2X) = 1/(2 · 0.5) = 1 p.u., at δ = 45° and U₂ = 0.707 p.u., far below the allowed 0.9 (p. 202).

practice.question: Both ends are held at 1 p.u., X = 0.5 p.u., and the angle between them is 30°. What active power flows?
practice.solution: P = U₁ U₂ sin δ / X = sin 30°/0.5 = 1 p.u.; the pull-out power at 90° is 2 p.u.

labs.title: Per-unit values
labs.idea: Divide every voltage, current and impedance by a base of its own kind and a network across several voltage levels becomes one circuit of numbers near 1. The base power is a free choice: it changes every per-unit value, never the current in amperes.

equations.eq: u = U/U_B, i = I/I_B, z = Z/Z_B
equations.note: per-unit values; only two bases are free, S_B = U_B I_B

equations.eq: X″_d = x″_d · U_B²/S_B
equations.note: a generator's subtransient reactance from its per-unit value

equations.eq: Z_Q = c U_n²/S″_kQ
equations.note: a feeding network from its short-circuit power

equations.eq: Z_T = u_k U_n²/S_n, R_T = P_k U_n²/S_n²
equations.note: the transformer in the example

equations.eq: z_new = z_old · (S_B,new/S_B,old) · (U_B,old/U_B,new)²
equations.note: a change of base, from the definitions
the fault current in amperes or per unit

practice.question: A generator of 80 MVA, 20 kV has x″d = 25 %. What is its subtransient reactance in ohms?
The 31 MVA transformer has u_k = 12 % on its own rating. What is its per-unit impedance on a 100 MVA base at the same voltage?
practice.solution: z = 0.12 · 100/31 = 0.387 p.u. In ohms nothing changes: 0.387 · (30 kV)²/100 MVA = 3.48 Ω either way.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Gawlik (2015), (6-33) and p. 215

labs.title: The short-circuit current
labs.idea: When a fault strikes, the current cannot jump to its new sine. A DC part starts where the sine would have to jump and decays with L/R; the first peak can reach almost twice the AC peak. Breakers and busbars are sized for it.
labs.law: i_p = κ √2 I″_k, κ = 1 + e^(−π R/X)

equations.eq: L di/dt + R i = √2 U sin(ωt + α)
equations.note: the fault switched on at angle α

equations.eq: i = √2 U/√(R² + ω²L²) [sin(ωt + α − φ) − sin(α − φ) e^(−t/T)]
equations.note: AC part plus decaying DC part

equations.eq: tan φ = ωL/R, T = L/R
I″_k3 = c U_n/(√3 Z_k), c = 1.1 above 1 kV
equations.note: initial symmetrical short-circuit current

equations.eq: i_p = √2 (1 + e^(−t R/L)) I″_k = κ √2 I″_k at t = 10 ms
equations.note: peak short-circuit current

practice.question: In the notes' example the fault path at 30 kV has R_k = 4.95 Ω and X_k = 17.68 Ω, with c = 1.1. What is I″k3?
Its R/X is 0.28. What peak factor κ does (6-43) give?
practice.solution: κ = 1 + e^(−π · 0.28) = 1 + 0.415 = 1.415; the notes read 1.4 off figure 6-18.

practice.question: What peak short-circuit current i_p follows?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Gawlik (2015), (6-43) and p. 216

labs.title: The power-angle curve and equal areas
labs.idea: During a fault the generator cannot deliver its turbine's power, so it speeds up and its angle grows. Once the fault is cleared it delivers more than the turbine gives and brakes. It stays in step only if the braking area can take back all the energy of the accelerating area.

equations.eq: P = 3 U_p U_N sin δ / X, X = X_G + X_T + X_L + X_N
equations.note: the generator on the network

equations.eq: stable on the rising side, δ < 90°; unstable on the falling side
A1 = ∫ from δ0 to δc of (P_m − P_fault(δ)) dδ
equations.note: accelerating area

equations.eq: A2 = ∫ from δc to δmax of (P_post(δ) − P_m) dδ
equations.note: braking area

equations.eq: A2 > A1
equations.note: the equal-area criterion; otherwise the generator slips

equations.eq: cos δcr = [P_m (δmax − δ0) + P_post cos δmax − P_fault cos δ0]/(P_post − P_fault)
equations.note: the critical clearing angle, from A1 = A2

practice.question: A turbine delivers 0.8 of the rating; over both lines the curve peaks at 1.6. At what angle does the generator run?
practice.solution: sin δ0 = 0.8/1.6 = 0.5, δ0 = 30°, on the rising side.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Gawlik (2015), (6-80), with example peaks

practice.question: A fault at the busbar transfers nothing; after clearing, one line remains with a peak of 1.2. What is the critical clearing angle?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Gawlik (2015), figure 6-45, with example peaks

labs.title: The rotating field
labs.idea: Each winding alone makes a field that only pulses along its axis. Three windings 120° apart, fed with currents 120° apart in time, add up to one field of constant strength that turns with the supply: the rotating field every AC machine runs on.
labs.law: i_s = ⅔ (i_u + i_v e^(j2π/3) + i_w e^(j4π/3))
labs.lecture: Schrödl (2012), pp. 11 and 149–155; Gawlik (2015), section 4.3, pp. 118–120

equations.eq: V_ges = const · J · N/2 in the real axis
equations.note: N windings with sinusoidal currents: N/2 times one winding's field

equations.eq: i = (2/N) Σ i_k e^(j2π(k−1)/N), i_k = J_k/(√2 J_Nenn)
equations.note: the per-unit current space vector

equations.eq: i = ⅔ (i₁ + i₂ e^(j2π/3) + i₃ e^(j4π/3))
equations.note: three phases

equations.eq: i_u = ½, i_v = −1, i_w = ½ gives i_s = 1 · e^(j300°)
equations.note: an instant of rated current

equations.eq: ψ_s = l_s i_s, l_s = 3/2 l_Strang
equations.note: the three-phase inductance is 3/2 the phase inductance

equations.eq: n_synch = 60 f/p [1/min]
equations.note: synchronous speed

equations.eq: s = (n_synch − n)/n_synch
equations.note: slip of an induction machine

practice.question: A hydro generator on the 50 Hz network turns at 375 min⁻¹. How many pole pairs does it have?
practice.solution: p = 60 f/n = 3000/375 = 8 pole pairs, 16 poles.

practice.question: A four-pole induction motor for 50 Hz runs at 1475 min⁻¹ at rated load. What is its slip?

labs.title: The DC machine's characteristics
labs.idea: The armature voltage sets the no-load speed, the load pulls it down a little through the armature resistance. Weakening the field raises the speed further but steepens the line and lowers the torque each ampere makes: constant torque below rated speed, constant power above.
labs.law: n = (U_A − J R_A)/(kΦ), M_i = kΦ J/2π

equations.eq: U_i,A = k Φ n, k = z p/a
equations.note: induced voltage, n in 1/s

equations.eq: M_i = (k/2π) Φ J
equations.note: internal torque

equations.eq: U_A = J R_A + k Φ n + L_A dJ/dt
equations.note: armature voltage equation, brush drop added to U_A

equations.eq: Θ_m dΩ_m/dt = k' Φ J + M_Last
equations.note: mechanical equation, k' = k/2π

equations.eq: n = Ω_m/2π = (U_A − J R_A)/(kΦ)
equations.note: steady state

equations.eq: (dω_m/di_A) = −r_A below rated speed, −r_A/φ in field weakening
equations.note: half the flux, twice the slope against current

equations.eq: i_A(ω_m = 0) = u_A/r_A
equations.note: every field-weakening line meets at standstill on the current axis

practice.question: A separately excited DC machine has I_N = 200 A, kΦ_N = 15 V·s, n_0 = 2000 min⁻¹ and n_N = 1960 min⁻¹. What is its armature resistance?
practice.source: Exam of 24 July 2013, worked solution, in VO-370.015 Prüfungen (2017)

practice.question: What is its rated torque?
practice.source: Exam of 24 July 2013, worked solution, in VO-370.015 Prüfungen (2017)

practice.question: The field is set to half. What torque can rated current now make?
practice.solution: Half the flux, half the torque per ampere: 7.5/(2π) · 200 = 238.73 N·m.
practice.source: Exam of 24 July 2013, worked solution, in VO-370.015 Prüfungen (2017)

practice.question: At 300 V and half field, what is its no-load speed?
practice.solution: n_0 = U_A/(kΦ) = 300 V/7.5 V·s = 40 s⁻¹ = 2400 min⁻¹. The line falls 0.335 min⁻¹ per N·m, four times as steep as at full field. (The worked solution prints 0.0559, and 2000 − 0.0837 M for full field at 300 V, whose 2000 belongs to 500 V; both slips are corrected here.)
practice.source: Exam of 24 July 2013, worked solution, in VO-370.015 Prüfungen (2017), checked by hand

practice.question: A permanent-magnet DC machine (48 V, 10 A, n_0 = 4000 min⁻¹ at 48 V, R_A = 0.3 Ω) runs at 3000 min⁻¹ with half its rated torque. What voltage must the converter supply?
practice.solution: kΦ = 48 V/(4000/60 s⁻¹) = 0.72 V·s. Half torque is half current, 5 A. U_A = J R_A + kΦ n = 1.5 V + 0.72 · 50 V = 37.5 V.
practice.source: Exercise in Schrödl (2012), p. 126, worked by hand

labs.title: The permanent-magnet synchronous machine
labs.idea: The magnet's flux sits on the rotor's d axis. Only the current at right angles to it, along q, makes torque; current along d only bends the stator flux. Seen from the rotor everything stands still, and one diagram of space vectors shows current, flux and the voltage the converter must supply.
labs.law: m = i_q |ψ_M|, u_s = r_s i_s + jω ψ_s

equations.eq: u_s = r_s i_s + dψ_s/dτ + jω_K ψ_s
equations.note: stator voltage in coordinates turning at ω_K

equations.eq: ψ_s = l_s i_s + ψ_M
equations.note: stator flux linkage

equations.eq: m = −Im(i_s* ψ_s)
equations.note: torque

equations.eq: m = i_sq ψ_Md − i_sd ψ_Mq = i_sq |ψ_M|
equations.note: in rotor coordinates; the d current makes no torque

equations.eq: u_Sd0 = i_Sd0 r_s, u_Sq0 = ω_U (l_s i_Sd0 + ψ_Md0)
equations.note: steady no-load voltage
the phase currents of a space vector

practice.question: The magnet's flux linkage is ψ_M = 1·e^(−j15°). In sine operation the machine is to give torque 1, motoring forwards. What is the per-unit current in lead u?
practice.source: Exam of 24 June 2013, worked solution, in VO-370.015 Prüfungen (2017)

practice.question: And the current in lead w?
practice.solution: i_w = Re{e^(j75°) e^(j120°)} = cos 195° = −0.966; i_v = cos(−45°) = 0.707, and the three sum to zero.
practice.source: Exam of 24 June 2013, worked solution, in VO-370.015 Prüfungen (2017)

practice.question: The machine runs unloaded with no current at speed 0.8. How large is its stator voltage?
practice.solution: With i_s = 0, u_Sd = 0 and u_Sq = ω ψ_M = 0.8: the magnet induces a voltage in proportion to speed.
